Argument for “North of the Desert” (Debater_A)

Main Thesis  
  • The text repeatedly places the spaceship’s landing site to the north of the “white waste of desert,” not to the west of the city. The city is seen from the landing point as lying to the west.

1. Textual Evidence: Relative Directions  
  • “Beneath them, the jagged peak of the mountain… To the south, beyond the rocks, lay a white waste of desert. To the west— ‘A city,’ yelled Nichols.”  
    – The desert lies to the south of the landing site; the city lies to the west. (quote)  
    – Therefore, they have landed north of the desert (because it is “beyond…to the south”) and east of the city (because the city is “to the west”).  
  • If the ship were west of the city, the text would read “To the east—” before revealing the city, which it does not.

2. Approach and Entry Sequence Confirms Eastward Position  
  • “The green beam… The section of the globe slid back, and the spaceship moved through the opening.”  
    – They move toward the city from their landing site, not away from it. Moving toward implies they were east of the city moving westward into it.  
  • They then secure sun-blasters at a ramp “stretching upward” while carrying “clean air” and “whitish mist” from the city back into their ship for testing, again implying proximity east of the city.

3. Logical Geography of the Planet  
  • The planet is described as a “dead planet” with white desert to the south and mountains flanking the valley. Irgi built his city in a more hospitable sector—presumably away from the harsh desert.  
    – The explorers land on a rocky plain “between two high, craggy mountains” then see the city beyond. Landing adjacent to mountains north of the desert fits well with their landing points in interplanetary navigation (avoiding open desert).  
  • If they landed west of the city, they would see desert on the far side of the city when approaching, but text never mentions desert beyond the city—only from the landing site.

4. Attack on “West of the City” Position (Debater_B)  
  • Misreads “To the west—‘A city’” as implying the landing site is west of the city. This line in fact indicates the city lies west of the observers.  
  • Offers no evidence of desert being north of or beyond the city; the city is always between the landing site and the desert.  
  • Contradicts the explorers’ subsequent movement “through the opening” into the city—as westward movement—from their landing point in the east, not eastward.  
  • Ignores the statement that the explorers “felt the green beam… lifting us” off the plain and depositing them “on the white flagging of an immense square,” i.e., the city’s plaza. Only plausible if they traveled westward into the city from the landing site in the plain.

5. Consistency with Irgi’s Discoveries  
  • Irgi brings the unconscious men “swiftly across the square” to his lab “next to the Chamber of the Cones.” If the explorers had been west of the city, he would have brought them back east into the plains, not toward his central power chamber in the city.  
  • The explorers’ bodies are “lifted” by Irgi from the city square “onto a flat, glittering ramp” leading into the city’s interior. That ramp faces toward the plain—i.e., eastward—again confirming they came west into the city.

Conclusion  
  All narrative evidence—directional markers (“to the south…to the west”), the explorers’ approach into the city, the geographic layout, and subsequent handling by Irgi—unambiguously show that the landing site was north of the desert and east of the city. The city was westward from the landing point, not vice versa. Therefore, “north of the desert” is the only correct answer.

A northward landing in desert requires a long traverse before such immediate admission.

4. Consistency with compass usage throughout  
   • All directional references are precise: “north… south… west.” Debater_A’s theory ignores repeated textual cues that “west” is synonymous with the city’s location relative to their landing point.

Refuting Debater_A’s “north of the desert”:

A. Misreads “north” reference  
   • Debater_A relies on “far to the north a mountain range…” but that range is from their vantage before landing; after landing, they see the city “to the west.” The landing point is south of those northern mountains.

B. Contradicts “white waste of desert… south”  
   • If they landed north of the desert, they would face desert to the south and city elsewhere; but text has the desert to their south “beyond the rocks” *before* they even land. They do not traverse southward to a landing—they already are on the plain.

C. Fails to explain “west—‘A city’” as immediate bearing  
   • Debater_A cannot explain why the first sighting of an inhabited area is west unless the ship swings or travels post-landing. Yet the narrative shows the globe opening immediately and the ship moving directly in, indicating no lateral traverse.

The desert lies to the south and the northern mountains guard the valley; from that valley, the astronauts “west” is the city’s entrance. The “west—‘A city’” exclamation is not a viewing of the desert from the city, but of the city from the plain.
